implication

/im-plih-KAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Implication means a probable consequence of something, often left unstated, or something suggested indirectly without being said outright.

The coach never said anyone was cut, but the shortened roster list carried an unmistakable implication.

Example

When the superintendent announced that next year's budget would 'prioritize programs with measurable outcomes,' she never mentioned the arts department. Teachers understood the implication at once: programs like band and theater, whose value is hard to measure on a test, would be the first to face cuts. Nothing was stated outright, yet the probable consequence was clear to everyone in the room.

The announcement never said that arts programs would be cut, but that probable consequence was suggested without being stated directly, which is exactly what an implication is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ramification: A ramification is a consequence that spreads outward from a decision, branching into areas nobody listed at the time. Implication is quieter and closer to the source: the probable consequence a statement or fact carries without saying it. Ramifications unfold out in the world; an implication sits inside the words, waiting to be read.

insinuation: An insinuation is an indirect suggestion with an edge — sly, usually unfriendly, hinting at something discreditable about someone. An implication can be perfectly neutral: a fact quietly carrying its probable consequence. Rising prices carry an implication about the budget; a raised eyebrow at the mention of a rival's name is an insinuation.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

declaration: an open, direct statement

Where it sits · how forcefully the message is delivered

hint → implication → accusation

hint vs. implication: A hint is a light, playful nudge toward an idea, while an implication carries a real message or consequence, even though it goes unsaid.

accusation vs. implication: An implication only suggests something indirectly, but an accusation states a charge openly and directly.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-: in, into (a form of in-)

Root — plic: from Latin plicare, to fold

Suffix — -ation: the act or result of

Put it together: Implication comes from Latin implicare, 'to fold in' or 'to entangle,' from in- (in) plus plicare (to fold). An implication is a meaning or consequence folded inside a statement, left for the listener to unfold.

Use the root in a new word: implicate: The muddy footprints seemed to implicate the gardener, folding him, as the Latin root plicare suggests, right into the middle of the mystery.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral to formal, academic and everyday register

Implication commonly appears in two patterns: 'the implications of' a decision or discovery (its probable consequences, often plural) and 'an implication that' something is true (a message suggested without being stated). Saying something 'by implication' means the listener must read between the lines.
